documents.title: Prepayment reference data set documentation – Dutch residential mortgages

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content and data quality of the reference data set RDS-PPM-NL-2026.1, which serves the Mortgage Prepayment Model NL (PPM-NL) version 3.0, registered in the model inventory under model identifier MDL-11. The RDS covers the EUR-denominated fixed-rate Dutch residential mortgage loan parts of the Bank and of its mortgage-label subsidiary that are serviced on the mortgage administration system (MAS). PPM-NL estimates monthly full and partial prepayment probabilities, rate-reset behaviour at the end of the fixed-rate period and the take-up of mortgage offers; its output is used in the EVE and NII measurement of interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB), the supervisory outlier tests (SOT), the ICAAP, the mortgage hedging programme and funds transfer pricing (FTP). The document follows the RDS template in Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0, as required by ALM-STD-400 §10.4, and the data quality of the RDS has been assessed under MRM-STD-022 (chapter 6). The RDS replaces RDS-PPM-NL-2022.2, which was used for PPM-NL v2.3.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains monthly loan-part snapshots from 31 January 2012 to 31 December 2025 (168 reference dates), comprising 171,612,448 loan-part-months for 1,962,305 unique loan parts of 834,117 unique mortgage loans, with 229,412 full prepayments (151,806 related to sale of the property and 77,606 to refinancing or other reasons), 1,384,066 partial prepayments and 512,334 ends of a fixed-rate period. At 31 December 2025 the in-scope portfolio consisted of 1,126,480 loan parts of 548,210 mortgage loans with an outstanding principal of EUR 98.6 billion. The long-run average conditional prepayment rate (CPR) over the observation period is 6.4% per year, of which 3.6 percentage points relate to full prepayment at sale, 1.1 percentage points to full prepayment for refinancing and 1.7 percentage points to partial prepayments; annual CPR ranged from 4.2% (2023) to 9.6% (2021). The pipeline component is estimated on a separate table of 412,650 mortgage offers issued between January 2016 and December 2025 (section 5.2).

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2012, the first month after the migration of the mortgage portfolio to MAS in 2011, and therefore covers the longest period with consistent loan-level redemption data. It includes the declining-rate period 2012–2021 with strongly positive refinancing incentives, the rising-rate period from mid-2022 to the end of 2023 in which most loan parts moved out of the money, and the moderate decline in 2024–2025, so that both positive and negative incentives are observed in the Bank's own data. It also covers the housing market recovery after 2013, the 2020–2021 pandemic period and the temporary increase of the gift tax exemption for home ownership between October 2013 and December 2014, which caused an exceptional level of partial prepayments (treated by expert judgement EJ-PPM-04 in the MDD). With 14 years of loan-level history the window exceeds the minimum of five years required by ALM-STD-400 §6.4.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable is the monthly prepayment outcome of each loan part, with four mutually exclusive categories: no prepayment, partial prepayment, full prepayment related to sale of the property, and full prepayment for refinancing or other reasons. A partial prepayment is an unscheduled principal repayment above EUR 250 in the month in excess of the contractual amortisation; smaller amounts are treated as rounding. Full prepayment is identified from redemption transactions (MAS transaction codes 410–418) that bring the loan-part balance to zero before the contractual maturity, and its reason is taken from the redemption reason code. The outcome horizon is one month; annual rates are derived as CPR = 1 − (1 − SMM)^12, where SMM is the single monthly mortality. Redemptions and rate resets at the end of the fixed-rate period are recorded in a separate event table, because the borrower can then repay without penalty and the drivers differ from those of prepayments during the fixed-rate period.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable: the target variable of PPM-NL is a prepayment event and not the regulatory default event, so there is no deviation from the definition of default in CR-STD-110 to report; the template heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. The Bank's definition of default is used only to identify non-performing loan parts for exclusion E1 (section 4.2), and it is applied without adjustment. Loan parts that return to performing status after the probation period re-enter the RDS population from the first month after the end of the probation period.

sections.text: Not applicable as a target definition. sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable: unlikeliness-to-pay triggers are relevant only to the construction of a default flag, and PPM-NL does not use a default-based target. The unlikeliness-to-pay status of a loan part enters the RDS only through the default register flag used for exclusion E1, which already reflects the UTP triggers of CR-STD-110 applied at obligor level by the arrears management system. No separate UTP data are therefore extracted, and no UTP-related data quality rules are defined for this RDS.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from six sources: MAS (loan-part master data, balances, contract rates, fixed-rate end dates, redemption transactions and reason codes), the default register (non-performing status), the collateral valuation database CVD (indexed market values), the mortgage pricing system MPS (historical offered rates per fixed-rate period, product and NHG class, and issued offers), the Market Data Hub (EUR swap and €STR curves) and the house price index for existing owner-occupied dwellings published monthly by Statistics Netherlands (CBS) and the Land Registry (Kadaster). For each type of data the authoritative source is defined in the Group Data Catalogue: MAS for contractual loan data, the default register for default and non-performing status, CVD for collateral values, MPS for offered rates and offers, and the Market Data Hub for market curves and the house price index. MAS records per loan part the fixed-rate end date (next repricing date), the interest rate type and product rate code, the embedded prepayment options (penalty-free allowance percentage and penalty-free events such as sale of the property, death of the borrower and redemption at the end of the fixed-rate period) and the basis of the prepayment compensation, and all of these fields are extracted into the RDS. The RDS covers all EUR fixed-rate residential mortgage loan parts of the Bank and of its mortgage-label subsidiary, which together represent the group's entire residential mortgage exposure. Source data are extracted from the month-end snapshots of the Finance Data Warehouse (FDW) and the ALM data mart (ALMDM); the extraction reference dates are listed in chapter 8 and the lineage per variable in Annex A.

sections.heading: Manual and external inputs
sections.text: The only manual input in the data flow is the offered-rate table for 2012–2013 for fixed-rate periods of 15 years and longer, which was reconstructed from archived rate sheets because MPS history for these products starts in January 2014; the reconstructed table is held as a version-controlled file (ref_data/offered_rates_2012_2013.csv, commit 4e1a9c2), was checked against the archived rate sheets by a second developer, and is identified in the lineage with this control. The reconstruction is documented as expert judgement in data treatment EJ-PPM-05, approved by the Model Owner on 14 October 2026 and cross-referenced to data deficiency DD-02. External data enter the lineage at the point of receipt within the Bank: the CBS/Kadaster house price index is received monthly through the Market Data Hub (data product PBK-NL, base year 2020 = 100, delivered around the 22nd of each month with the delivery date recorded), and swap and €STR curves are received from the Bank's market data vendor feed with the delivery date recorded per curve.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Four exclusions are applied; counts refer to loan-part-months of the observation period. E1 – non-performing loan parts (in default or more than 90 days past due at the reference date): 1,905,210 loan-part-months (1.1%), excluded because redemption is then driven by the workout process rather than borrower choice; these exposures are included in IRRBB measurement with the expected cash flows of the workout model (MDD section 2.4). E2 – staff mortgages with preferential pricing: 1,441,880 loan-part-months (0.8%), excluded because the staff discount removes the refinancing incentive. E3 – records with technical balance movements (loan-part splits, product conversions and administrative corrections, transaction codes 820–829): 1,013,540 loan-part-months (0.6%). E4 – the first month after origination: 1,952,020 loan-part-months (1.1%), excluded because construction-deposit loans are not yet fully drawn. For each exclusion the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that it does not materially change the risk-driver distributions or the prepayment rates of the retained population (largest effect: E1, +0.07 percentage points on the portfolio CPR). Variable-rate loan parts (2.4% of balances) reprice monthly and are outside the scope of the model rather than excluded from it.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, values missing for a structural reason and values missing because of a data deficiency. Borrower date of birth is missing for 1.9% of loan parts (DD-04) and is imputed with the median age of the origination-year and product cohort; the original principal is missing for 0.8% of migrated loan parts (DD-03) and is replaced by the earliest observed balance; the indexed market value is structurally missing for 0.3% of loan parts without a valuation in CVD and is derived from the origination value indexed with the regional house price index. All imputations are performed by build code (rds/impute.py) with fixed rules, the share of imputed values per variable is reported in Annex C, and re-estimation without the imputed records changed no coefficient by more than 3% and the portfolio CPR by less than 0.02 percentage points. Outliers are identified by documented rules that are applied identically in the RDS build and in production: contract rates outside 0%–12%, indexed LTV above 250% and partial prepayment amounts above the outstanding balance. Indexed LTV is capped at 250%, affecting 0.02% of loan-part-months with no measurable effect on the estimated CPR, and contract rates outside the permitted range are set to missing and investigated. The target variable is never imputed: 3,412 redemption records with inconsistent amounts were investigated with Mortgage Operations, 3,108 were corrected at source in MAS and the remaining 304 were excluded under E3.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: The RDS contains the full in-scope portfolio at every reference date, so representativeness concerns the stability of the portfolio and of borrower behaviour over time rather than sample selection. The risk-driver distributions of the RDS were compared with the portfolio at 31 December 2025 using the PSI: loan type 0.03, remaining fixed-rate period 0.06, seasoning 0.08, indexed LTV 0.12 and refinancing incentive 0.41 (Annex B). The high PSI of the refinancing incentive is expected, because the incentive distribution is driven by the rate environment: at 31 December 2025, 64% of the balance was out of the money against an RDS average of 31%; the RDS nevertheless contains 38.2 million loan-part-months with a negative incentive, mainly from 2022–2025, which supports estimation of the out-of-the-money response on the Bank's own data. On outcome levels, the realised 2025 CPR of the portfolio (5.1%) lies within the range observed in the RDS, and the segment CPRs of 2025 lie within the range of annual segment CPRs in the RDS.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The pipeline take-up component is estimated on the offer table of the RDS, which contains the 412,650 mortgage offers issued by MPS between January 2016 and December 2025 with offer date, offered rate, fixed-rate period, offer validity and the drawdown or expiry outcome. Offers before 2016 are not available in MPS in a consistent form, and the offer table therefore covers ten years including the 2022–2023 period of rapidly rising rates, in which the take-up of outstanding offers peaked at 93%. Together with the loan-part table, the offer table ensures that the model perimeter covers both drawn fixed-rate mortgages and the off-balance-sheet loan commitments arising from issued offers. The use of model outputs for FTP and hedge accounting relates to the same population as the RDS, so no further representativeness analysis is required for these uses.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Re-running the estimation with each exclusion reversed changes the portfolio CPR by +0.07 percentage points (E1), +0.01 percentage points (E2), −0.02 percentage points (E3) and less than 0.01 percentage points (E4), and changes the PSI of no risk driver by more than 0.01. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records or of exposure in any segment (the largest share is E1 in the interest-only segment with 1.9% of loan-part-months and 2.1% of exposure), so Model Owner approval under MRM-STD-022 §5.3 was not required; the exclusions are justified, quantified and reported to Model Validation in this document. The conclusion is that the retained population is representative of the in-scope portfolio for all three segments.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The DQ assessment of RDS-PPM-NL-2026.1 was performed between 5 and 30 October 2026, before model estimation started, applying MRM-STD-022 and the DQ rules agreed with the Data Owners. Data quality is assessed on the four mandatory dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness for all 17 CDEs, and additionally on validity and uniqueness; appropriateness is covered by chapter 5. The results per rule are reported in the data quality assessment report EVD-11-DQR, of which the main results are summarised in sections 6.1.1 to 6.1.3. The assessment was performed by ALM Modelling with the Data Stewards of the four data domains.

sections.heading: DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: A total of 96 DQ rules are defined for the 17 CDEs, with at least one rule per applicable mandatory dimension; timeliness is recorded as not applicable to static origination attributes (origination date and original principal), with the reason stated in Annex C. The rules are documented in Annex A, and the 71 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool as rule set DQM-ALM-PPM. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: completeness amber below 98% and red below 95%, reconciliation differences amber above 0.5% and red above 1% of amount, and logical consistency amber below 99% and red below 98% of records passing. For the target constituents (redemption amount, redemption transaction code and redemption reason code) stricter thresholds apply: completeness amber below 99.5% and red below 99%, and reconciliation of redemption amounts to the general ledger amber above 0.1% and red above 0.25%. One deviation applies: the completeness threshold for the redemption reason code is relaxed for reference dates in 2012–2015 to amber below 80% and red below 70%, justified by the historical data gap DD-01 and approved by the Model Owner on 21 October 2026 and by Model Risk Management on 23 October 2026 (MRM-DEV-2026-044).

sections.heading: Data minimisation, pseudonymisation and security
sections.text: Personal data use in the RDS is limited to the attributes listed in Annex A, each justified by its relevance to prepayment behaviour, and is covered by DPIA-2026-142: borrower age drives relocation and prepayment from savings, and the province is used only to map the regional house price index, while names, addresses, full postcodes, income and employment data are not extracted. sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content and data quality of the reference data set RDS-PPM-NL-2026.1, which serves the Mortgage Prepayment Model NL (PPM-NL) version 3.0, registered in the model inventory under model identifier MDL-11. The RDS covers the EUR-denominated fixed-rate Dutch residential mortgage loan parts of the Bank and of its mortgage-label subsidiary that are serviced on the mortgage administration system (MAS). PPM-NL estimates monthly full and partial prepayment probabilities, rate-reset behaviour at the end of the fixed-rate period and the take-up of mortgage offers; its output is used in the EVE and NII measurement of interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB), the supervisory outlier tests (SOT), the ICAAP, the mortgage hedging programme and funds transfer pricing (FTP). The document follows the RDS template in Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0, as required by ALM-STD-400 §10.4, and the data quality of the RDS has been assessed under MRM-STD-022 (chapter 6). The RDS replaces RDS-PPM-NL-2022.2, which was used for PPM-NL v2.3.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2012, the first month after the migration of the mortgage portfolio to MAS in 2011, and therefore covers the longest period with consistent loan-level redemption data. It includes the declining-rate period 2012–2021 with strongly positive refinancing incentives, the rising-rate period from mid-2022 to the end of 2023 in which most loan parts moved out of the money, and the moderate decline in 2024–2025, so that both positive and negative incentives are observed in the Bank's own data. It also covers the housing market recovery after 2013, the 2020–2021 pandemic period and the temporary increase of the gift tax exemption for home ownership between October 2013 and December 2014, which caused an exceptional level of partial prepayments (treated by expert judgement EJ-PPM-04 in the MDD). With 14 years of loan-level history the window exceeds the minimum of five years required by ALM-STD-400 §6.4.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable is the monthly prepayment outcome of each loan part, with four mutually exclusive categories: no prepayment, partial prepayment, full prepayment related to sale of the property, and full prepayment for refinancing or other reasons. A partial prepayment is an unscheduled principal repayment above EUR 250 in the month in excess of the contractual amortisation; smaller amounts are treated as rounding. Full prepayment is identified from redemption transactions (MAS transaction codes 410–418) that bring the loan-part balance to zero before the contractual maturity, and its reason is taken from the redemption reason code. The outcome horizon is one month; annual rates are derived as CPR = 1 − (1 − SMM)^12, where SMM is the single monthly mortality. Redemptions and rate resets at the end of the fixed-rate period are recorded in a separate event table, because the borrower can then repay without penalty and the drivers differ from those of prepayments during the fixed-rate period.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable: unlikeliness-to-pay triggers are relevant only to the construction of a default flag, and PPM-NL does not use a default-based target. sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from six sources: MAS (loan-part master data, balances, contract rates, fixed-rate end dates, redemption transactions and reason codes), the default register (non-performing status), the collateral valuation database CVD (indexed market values), the mortgage pricing system MPS (historical offered rates per fixed-rate period, product and NHG class, and issued offers), the Market Data Hub (EUR swap and €STR curves) and the house price index for existing owner-occupied dwellings published monthly by Statistics Netherlands (CBS) and the Land Registry (Kadaster). For each type of data the authoritative source is defined in the Group Data Catalogue: MAS for contractual loan data, the default register for default and non-performing status, CVD for collateral values, MPS for offered rates and offers, and the Market Data Hub for market curves and the house price index. MAS records per loan part the fixed-rate end date (next repricing date), the interest rate type and product rate code, the embedded prepayment options (penalty-free allowance percentage and penalty-free events such as sale of the property, death of the borrower and redemption at the end of the fixed-rate period) and the basis of the prepayment compensation, and all of these fields are extracted into the RDS. The RDS covers all EUR fixed-rate residential mortgage loan parts of the Bank and of its mortgage-label subsidiary, which together represent the group's entire residential mortgage exposure. Source data are extracted from the month-end snapshots of the Finance Data Warehouse (FDW) and the ALM data mart (ALMDM); the extraction reference dates are listed in chapter 8 and the lineage per variable in Annex A.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Four exclusions are applied; counts refer to loan-part-months of the observation period. E1 – non-performing loan parts (in default or more than 90 days past due at the reference date): 1,905,210 loan-part-months (1.1%), excluded because redemption is then driven by the workout process rather than borrower choice; these exposures are included in IRRBB measurement with the expected cash flows of the workout model (MDD section 2.4). E2 – staff mortgages with preferential pricing: 1,441,880 loan-part-months (0.8%), excluded because the staff discount removes the refinancing incentive. E3 – records with technical balance movements (loan-part splits, product conversions and administrative corrections, transaction codes 820–829): 1,013,540 loan-part-months (0.6%). E4 – the first month after origination: 1,952,020 loan-part-months (1.1%), excluded because construction-deposit loans are not yet fully drawn. For each exclusion the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that it does not materially change the risk-driver distributions or the prepayment rates of the retained population (largest effect: E1, +0.07 percentage points on the portfolio CPR). Variable-rate loan parts (2.4% of balances) reprice monthly and are outside the scope of the model rather than excluded from it.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, values missing for a structural reason and values missing because of a data deficiency. Borrower date of birth is missing for 1.9% of loan parts (DD-04) and is imputed with the median age of the origination-year and product cohort; the original principal is missing for 0.8% of migrated loan parts (DD-03) and is replaced by the earliest observed balance; the indexed market value is structurally missing for 0.3% of loan parts without a valuation in CVD and is derived from the origination value indexed with the regional house price index. All imputations are performed by build code (rds/impute.py) with fixed rules, the share of imputed values per variable is reported in Annex C, and re-estimation without the imputed records changed no coefficient by more than 3% and the portfolio CPR by less than 0.02 percentage points. Outliers are identified by documented rules that are applied identically in the RDS build and in production: contract rates outside 0%–12%, indexed LTV above 250% and partial prepayment amounts above the outstanding balance. Indexed LTV is capped at 250%, affecting 0.02% of loan-part-months with no measurable effect on the estimated CPR, and contract rates outside the permitted range are set to missing and investigated. The target variable is never imputed: 3,412 redemption records with inconsistent amounts were investigated with Mortgage Operations, 3,108 were corrected at source in MAS and the remaining 304 were excluded under E3.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: The RDS contains the full in-scope portfolio at every reference date, so representativeness concerns the stability of the portfolio and of borrower behaviour over time rather than sample selection. The risk-driver distributions of the RDS were compared with the portfolio at 31 December 2025 using the PSI: loan type 0.03, remaining fixed-rate period 0.06, seasoning 0.08, indexed LTV 0.12 and refinancing incentive 0.41 (Annex B). The high PSI of the refinancing incentive is expected, because the incentive distribution is driven by the rate environment: at 31 December 2025, 64% of the balance was out of the money against an RDS average of 31%; the RDS nevertheless contains 38.2 million loan-part-months with a negative incentive, mainly from 2022–2025, which supports estimation of the out-of-the-money response on the Bank's own data. On outcome levels, the realised 2025 CPR of the portfolio (5.1%) lies within the range observed in the RDS, and the segment CPRs of 2025 lie within the range of annual segment CPRs in the RDS.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The pipeline take-up component is estimated on the offer table of the RDS, which contains the 412,650 mortgage offers issued by MPS between January 2016 and December 2025 with offer date, offered rate, fixed-rate period, offer validity and the drawdown or expiry outcome. Offers before 2016 are not available in MPS in a consistent form, and the offer table therefore covers ten years including the 2022–2023 period of rapidly rising rates, in which the take-up of outstanding offers peaked at 93%. Together with the loan-part table, the offer table ensures that the model perimeter covers both drawn fixed-rate mortgages and the off-balance-sheet loan commitments arising from issued offers. The use of model outputs for FTP and hedge accounting relates to the same population as the RDS, so no further representativeness analysis is required for these uses.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Re-running the estimation with each exclusion reversed changes the portfolio CPR by +0.07 percentage points (E1), +0.01 percentage points (E2), −0.02 percentage points (E3) and less than 0.01 percentage points (E4), and changes the PSI of no risk driver by more than 0.01. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records or of exposure in any segment (the largest share is E1 in the interest-only segment with 1.9% of loan-part-months and 2.1% of exposure), so Model Owner approval under MRM-STD-022 §5.3 was not required; the exclusions are justified, quantified and reported to Model Validation in this document. The conclusion is that the retained population is representative of the in-scope portfolio for all three segments.

sections.heading: DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: A total of 96 DQ rules are defined for the 17 CDEs, with at least one rule per applicable mandatory dimension; timeliness is recorded as not applicable to static origination attributes (origination date and original principal), with the reason stated in Annex C. The rules are documented in Annex A, and the 71 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool as rule set DQM-ALM-PPM. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: completeness amber below 98% and red below 95%, reconciliation differences amber above 0.5% and red above 1% of amount, and logical consistency amber below 99% and red below 98% of records passing. For the target constituents (redemption amount, redemption transaction code and redemption reason code) stricter thresholds apply: completeness amber below 99.5% and red below 99%, and reconciliation of redemption amounts to the general ledger amber above 0.1% and red above 0.25%. One deviation applies: the completeness threshold for the redemption reason code is relaxed for reference dates in 2012–2015 to amber below 80% and red below 70%, justified by the historical data gap DD-01 and approved by the Model Owner on 21 October 2026 and by Model Risk Management on 23 October 2026 (MRM-DEV-2026-044).

sections.text: DD-01 (completeness): the redemption reason code is missing for 17.6% of full prepayments in 2012–2015 because the field was optional in the legacy redemption process; the reason is derived by matching the redemption with a collateral release registered as sale in CVD, residual cases being assigned to refinancing (EJ-PPM-06); impact: the sale/refinancing split is uncertain for 4.1% of all full prepayments; owner: Data Steward Retail Mortgages; limitation L-04. sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: PPM-NL v3.0 estimates scenario-dependent prepayment behaviour of the Bank's fixed-rate Dutch residential mortgages; it is a model under MRM-POL-001 §3 because its quantitative output is used for risk measurement, hedging decisions and regulatory reporting, and it is managed across the full model lifecycle. The intended uses are the projection of mortgage cash flows for EVE and NII measurement, the supervisory outlier tests, the ICAAP internal capital for IRRBB and the hedging of the mortgage portfolio by the Treasury ALM desk; secondary uses are funds transfer pricing and the hedge effectiveness testing of the mortgage fair value hedge. The range of application is the EUR fixed-rate residential mortgage portfolio serviced on MAS (EUR 98.6 billion at 31 December 2025) and the mortgage offer pipeline; variable-rate loan parts, consumer loans and non-performing loan parts are outside the range of application. The model is used for IRRBB measurement and is Tier 1 (section 1.2). Version 3.0 is a redevelopment of v2.3, which was approved by the MRC after a full-scope validation in June 2023, has been in production since the reference date 30 June 2023 and was assessed 'fit for purpose with conditions' at its 2026 annual validation.

sections.heading: Development plan and requirement set
sections.text: The development plan DP-PPM-2026-01 stated the purpose, intended use, scope, applicable requirements, data sources, candidate methodologies (section 4.1), planned performance and sensitivity tests, timeline and roles, and was approved by the model owner on 15 July 2026 before development started. sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: PPM-NL is a conditional (scenario-dependent) cash-flow model: prepayment probabilities are recomputed for every interest rate path of every EVE, NII and SOT scenario rather than taken as fixed unconditional CPR vectors. It consists of five components: (A) a monthly multinomial logit model for the outcomes no prepayment, partial prepayment, full prepayment at sale and full prepayment for refinancing; (B) a partial prepayment amount model; (C) a rate-reset model for the end of the fixed-rate period; (D) a projection module that converts loan-part probabilities into scenario-dependent SMM and CPR vectors and prepayment compensation; and (E) a pipeline take-up model for issued offers. Component D passes the vectors to the Bank's ALM engine, which generates the contractual and behavioural cash flows and computes EVE and NII. Full prepayments, partial prepayments and rate resets at the end of the fixed-rate period are modelled separately because their drivers differ: full prepayments at sale are driven by relocation, full prepayments for refinancing by the rate incentive net of compensation, partial prepayments by the penalty-free allowance and the return on savings, and rate resets by the Bank's offered rate at reset.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: The portfolio is divided into three behaviourally homogeneous segments by repayment type: S1 annuity and linear loan parts (EUR 71.3 billion, 72% of the balance at 31 December 2025), S2 interest-only loan parts (EUR 21.9 billion, 22%) and S3 savings- and investment-linked loan parts (EUR 5.4 billion, 6%). The segments differ in prepayment behaviour (2012–2025 average CPR 6.9%, 5.3% and 5.0% respectively) because interest-only borrowers are older and prepay mainly at sale, while savings-linked loan parts are redeemed from the linked account at maturity; separate intercepts and driver interactions are estimated per segment, and NHG guarantee, fixed-rate period and loan size enter as drivers rather than as segments. Segment homogeneity was tested with likelihood-ratio tests of pooled against segment-specific coefficients (p < 0.001 for S1 against S2 and S3).

sections.heading: Use in EVE measurement and the supervisory outlier test
sections.text: The EVE supervisory outlier test is computed quarterly for the six scenarios parallel up, parallel down, steepener, flattener, short rates up and short rates down, using the scenario-dependent CPR of PPM-NL. The Bank applies the EUR shock sizes of Part A of the Annex to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/856 (parallel 200 bp, short 250 bp, long 100 bp); no Part B calibration is needed because no other currency is material. EUR represents 98.7% of non-trading book financial assets and 97.9% of liabilities, USD (0.8%) and GBP (0.4%) are below the 5% threshold and EUR alone exceeds 90% coverage, so shocks are applied to EUR only; the model concerns EUR mortgages only. The change in EVE is computed on a run-off balance sheet in which existing loan parts amortise and prepay according to the scenario-dependent prepayment rates without new production. Cash flows are discounted with the EUR €STR OIS curve, a general risk-free curve without instrument-, sector- or entity-specific credit or liquidity spreads. As EUR is the only currency in scope, no cross-currency aggregation is needed; the ALM engine nevertheless applies the aggregation rule of Article 3(8), so a positive EVE change in a scenario is weighted by 50%.

sections.heading: Commercial margins and non-performing exposures
sections.text: For the EVE measures the Bank excludes commercial margins from the mortgage cash flows: interest cash flows are projected at the risk-free rate at inception, defined as the EUR OIS swap rate for the initial fixed-rate period at the offer date as used in FTP, applied consistently to all banking book instruments and business units and aligned with the hedging of the mortgage portfolio with OIS payer swaps; the exclusion was notified to the ECB Joint Supervisory Team on 28 June 2024. Non-performing mortgage loan parts (1.1% of the mortgage balance) are not modelled by PPM-NL but are included in EVE and NII as interest rate sensitive instruments, net of provisions, with the expected cash flows and timing of the workout model. The Bank's NPE ratio of 1.3% at 31 December 2026 is below 2%, so Article 3(4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/856 does not require the inclusion of NPEs in the SOT; they are nevertheless included to keep the SOT consistent with the internal measures. The IRRBB perimeter therefore covers all interest rate sensitive mortgage positions: performing and non-performing loan parts, the mortgage pipeline as off-balance-sheet loan commitments, and the related hedging derivatives.

sections.heading: Use in NII measurement
sections.text: The NII supervisory outlier test applies the parallel up and parallel down scenarios and covers interest income and expenses over a one-year horizon regardless of the maturity and accounting treatment of the instruments. The change in NII is computed on a constant balance sheet: prepaid, maturing and repricing mortgage balances are replaced by mortgages of the same currency, amount and fixed-rate period, priced at the average margin of new production over the last three months rather than at historical margins. The NII measures include commercial margins, and prepayment compensation received under each scenario is included in projected interest income. The NII outlier test flags a large decline where one-year NII falls by more than 5% of Tier 1 capital under either parallel scenario; with PPM-NL v3.0 the worst outcome at 31 December 2026 is −3.0% of Tier 1 capital (parallel down). The Bank uses the NII sensitivity including market value changes of fair-valued hedging instruments (NII+MV) and the EVE sensitivity, which together capture gap, basis and option risk; PPM-NL provides the option risk component of both measures.

sections.heading: Scenario-conditional application and rate floor
sections.text: Prepayment speeds respond to the rate path of each EVE, NII and SOT scenario: the refinancing incentive, the curtailment incentive and the lock-in effect on sales are recomputed monthly from the shocked offered-rate curve, so that prepayments rise in falling-rate scenarios and fall in rising-rate scenarios. After each shock, the post-shock rate floor of −150 bp at immediate maturity, rising by 3 bp per year to 0% at 50 years, is applied to the EUR risk-free curve before the offered rates and incentives are derived; where observed rates are below the floor, the observed rate is used. The application of PPM-NL to the prescribed shock scenarios, including the rate floor and the post-shock prepayment behaviour, was tested for all eight SOT scenarios in the parallel run (EVD-11-ITR section 7) and in the SOT comparison of EVD-11-BTR. IRRBB exposure is measured monthly under the internal set of 12 scenarios for changes in level and shape of the yield curve and in the basis between swap and mortgage offered rates, and the SOT quarterly. The same model and parameters are used for EVE, NII, the SOT, the ICAAP and hedging; FTP will continue to use the v2.3 CPR tables until the FTP system release planned for the first quarter of 2028.

sections.heading: Fixed-rate loans, prepayment compensation and pipeline
sections.text: For fixed-rate mortgage loan parts, the scenario-dependent prepayment rates, the rate-reset behaviour and the prepayment compensation are applied in every IRRBB measure; for fixed-rate loan commitments the expected take-up of the pipeline component is applied in all measures. The projection reflects the contractual prepayment conditions: a penalty-free allowance of 10% of the original principal per calendar year applies to all loan parts, prepayments at sale, death and at the end of the fixed-rate period are penalty-free, and other prepayments above the allowance pay compensation equal to the present value of the difference between the contract rate and the Bank's offered rate for the remaining fixed-rate period; the compensation received is included in projected NII and in the EVE cash flows. The pipeline take-up component estimates the probability that an offer is drawn as a logistic function of the change in the offered rate for the same fixed-rate period since the offer date and the remaining offer validity (offers are valid for six months, with the day-rate option that the borrower receives the lower of the offered and the prevailing rate at drawdown). Pipeline exposures are included in EVE, NII and the hedging strategy from the offer date with the expected take-up under each rate scenario, and the Treasury ALM desk hedges the expected pipeline with forward-starting payer swaps.

sections.text: Before estimation, the samples were defined as follows: the development window is January 2012 to December 2024; within it, 25% of mortgage loans were drawn at random (seed 20261109) as out-of-sample hold-out, and the out-of-time sample is January to December 2025 (12.1 million loan-part-months). sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Four methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements of ALM-STD-400 §6, data requirements, out-of-time accuracy, stability of the incentive response, interpretability and implementability in the ALM engine): (1) CPR look-up tables by incentive and seasoning bucket as in v2.3; (2) a Cox proportional hazards model; (3) a multinomial logit model; and (4) gradient-boosted trees. The look-up tables could not separate sale from refinancing and showed a 2025 out-of-time CPR error of +1.8 percentage points; the Cox model had a similar fit to the logit (AUC 0.719 against 0.726) but requires a baseline hazard that cannot be projected per scenario without additional assumptions; gradient-boosted trees improved the out-of-time AUC by only 0.006 and would be less transparent. The multinomial logit model was selected because it models the competing outcomes jointly, gives interpretable driver effects that can be challenged by Treasury, performs at least as well as the alternatives out of time, and can be applied per scenario in the projection module; the more complex gradient-boosted alternative was rejected as its small performance gain does not justify the loss of transparency.

sections.heading: Model specification
sections.text: For loan part i in month t, the probability of outcome k ∈ {partial prepayment, full prepayment at sale, full prepayment for refinancing} is P(k) = exp(β_k·x_it) / (1 + Σ_j exp(β_j·x_it)), with no prepayment as the reference outcome. The driver vector x_it contains segment intercepts, linear splines of the refinancing incentive, seasoning splines, the remaining penalty-free allowance, a December indicator, the curtailment incentive, borrower age band, the 12-month change in the regional house price index, indexed LTV bucket, remaining fixed-rate period bucket, a burnout variable, NHG indicator and loan size bucket. Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood with robust standard errors clustered by mortgage loan, using statsmodels MNLogit. The monthly probabilities are aggregated into the SMM per segment and scenario and converted to annual CPR.

sections.heading: Candidate drivers and variable selection
sections.text: Thirty-one candidate drivers were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the monthly production run and stability of their effect over 2012–2018 against 2019–2024; eight were rejected, for example the borrower's employment status (not available at the point of use) and the 3-month change in Euribor (effect not stable over time). Variable selection combined univariate analysis (information value per outcome), stepwise multivariate selection by likelihood-ratio test at 1% significance, and a correlation analysis in which, of pairs with a correlation above 0.6 (for example loan age and seasoning since the last rate reset), only the driver with the stronger economic rationale was retained. The final model uses as drivers the refinancing incentive, loan seasoning, the remaining penalty-free allowance, and relocation and property sale through borrower age, the regional house price change and the rate lock-in effect. Selection decisions that required judgement, such as the knot positions of the incentive spline, are recorded in the expert judgement log (chapter 11).

sections.heading: Final coefficients and economic rationale
sections.text: Every final driver has a sign and magnitude consistent with economic intuition: for refinancing, the incentive coefficient is +1.08 per 100 bp above the +50 bp knot and +0.21 per 100 bp between −100 bp and +50 bp, reflecting the threshold created by prepayment compensation; burnout reduces refinancing by −0.34 per year of cumulative in-the-money exposure; for sale, the house price change coefficient is +0.021 per percentage point, the lock-in effect is −0.18 per 100 bp of negative incentive and borrowers aged 25–34 move more often (+0.41 against age 45–54); for partial prepayment, the December indicator is +1.37, the remaining allowance +0.88 and the curtailment incentive +0.29 per 100 bp. sections.heading: Partial prepayment amount and rate reset
sections.text: Component B models the prepaid amount, as a share of the outstanding balance, given a partial prepayment, with a fractional logit on the remaining allowance, December indicator, age band and loan size; the median prepaid share is 4.8% and 71% of partial prepayments fall within the penalty-free allowance. Component C models, at the end of the fixed-rate period, the probability that the loan part is redeemed (on average 6.8% of resets in 2016–2025) as a logistic function of the difference between the Bank's offered rate and the market average rate, and the choice of the new fixed-rate period (2016–2025 average: 10 years 46%, 20 years 22%, 5 years 18%, one year or variable 14%) as a multinomial logit on the slope of the offered-rate curve. Internal refinancing through rate averaging during the fixed-rate period is treated as a refinancing event, because the loan part reprices to a new fixed-rate period. Both components are re-evaluated per scenario in the projection.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The calibration target is the realised monthly prepayment rate per segment on the development sample; the maximum likelihood estimates reproduce the in-sample full and partial prepayment rates per segment within 0.5% relative, so no separate recalibration step is applied. Prepayment parameters are calibrated on 13 years of loan-level history (2012–2024) and are recalibrated when the annual back-testing shows a structural deviation, defined as a red back-testing result in two consecutive years or in the latest year for the portfolio. sections.text: Performance was tested on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples for discriminatory power (AUC per outcome), calibration accuracy (predicted against realised CPR) and stability (PSI and coefficient stability), with metrics and thresholds consistent with MV-HB-003 and the monitoring plan. sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, PPM-NL v3.0 was compared with a challenger model (the Cox proportional hazards model of section 4) and with two benchmarks, the production model v2.3 and the average 2025 CPR of Dutch prime RMBS pools published in investor reports (5.6%). Out of time, the challenger gives a portfolio CPR of 5.5% and an AUC of 0.719, v2.3 gives 6.9% including its overlay (8.4% without), and v3.0 gives 5.3% against a realised 5.1%. The difference with v2.3 is explained by its bucket structure, which extrapolates the refinancing response of 2016–2021 and cannot represent the lock-in effect on sales; the difference with the RMBS benchmark is explained by the higher share of interest-only loans in the Bank's portfolio; the challenger does not outperform v3.0 on any material metric.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material model assumptions have been identified and assessed for plausibility: (a) borrower behaviour observed in 2012–2024 is representative of future behaviour conditional on the drivers; (b) the incentive response is stable and can be applied to shocked rate paths up to the observed incentive range; (c) the Bank's offered rate follows the swap curve with a constant margin in all scenarios; (d) the penalty-free allowance and compensation rules remain unchanged; (e) the intended use is portfolio-level projection and not loan-level prediction. The key behavioural assumptions are documented in this MDD, justified by the Bank's historical data (chapters 4, 5 and 7), aligned with the mortgage business strategy agreed with Mortgage Product Management, and tested annually through back-testing and sensitivity analysis; the materiality thresholds of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/857 are applied proportionately to decide which assumptions are modelled per scenario. All model inputs, assumptions and specification choices are documented and explained in chapters 3, 4 and 8 so that they are included in the independent validation.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: PPM-NL v3.0 estimates scenario-dependent prepayment behaviour of the Bank's fixed-rate Dutch residential mortgages; it is a model under MRM-POL-001 §3 because its quantitative output is used for risk measurement, hedging decisions and regulatory reporting, and it is managed across the full model lifecycle. The range of application is the EUR fixed-rate residential mortgage portfolio serviced on MAS (EUR 98.6 billion at 31 December 2025) and the mortgage offer pipeline; variable-rate loan parts, consumer loans and non-performing loan parts are outside the range of application. The model is used for IRRBB measurement and is Tier 1 (section 1.2). Version 3.0 is a redevelopment of v2.3, which was approved by the MRC after a full-scope validation in June 2023, has been in production since the reference date 30 June 2023 and was assessed 'fit for purpose with conditions' at its 2026 annual validation.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: PPM-NL is a conditional (scenario-dependent) cash-flow model: prepayment probabilities are recomputed for every interest rate path of every EVE, NII and SOT scenario rather than taken as fixed unconditional CPR vectors. It consists of five components: (A) a monthly multinomial logit model for the outcomes no prepayment, partial prepayment, full prepayment at sale and full prepayment for refinancing; (B) a partial prepayment amount model; (C) a rate-reset model for the end of the fixed-rate period; (D) a projection module that converts loan-part probabilities into scenario-dependent SMM and CPR vectors and prepayment compensation; and (E) a pipeline take-up model for issued offers. Component D passes the vectors to the Bank's ALM engine, which generates the contractual and behavioural cash flows and computes EVE and NII. Full prepayments, partial prepayments and rate resets at the end of the fixed-rate period are modelled separately because their drivers differ: full prepayments at sale are driven by relocation, full prepayments for refinancing by the rate incentive net of compensation, partial prepayments by the penalty-free allowance and the return on savings, and rate resets by the Bank's offered rate at reset.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: The portfolio is divided into three behaviourally homogeneous segments by repayment type: S1 annuity and linear loan parts (EUR 71.3 billion, 72% of the balance at 31 December 2025), S2 interest-only loan parts (EUR 21.9 billion, 22%) and S3 savings- and investment-linked loan parts (EUR 5.4 billion, 6%). The segments differ in prepayment behaviour (2012–2025 average CPR 6.9%, 5.3% and 5.0% respectively) because interest-only borrowers are older and prepay mainly at sale, while savings-linked loan parts are redeemed from the linked account at maturity; separate intercepts and driver interactions are estimated per segment, and NHG guarantee, fixed-rate period and loan size enter as drivers rather than as segments. Segment homogeneity was tested with likelihood-ratio tests of pooled against segment-specific coefficients (p < 0.001 for S1 against S2 and S3).

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and systems
sections.text: PPM-NL is developed internally and is managed under MRM-POL-001; the vendor ALM engine that converts the CPR vectors into cash flows is registered in the tools register as TOOL-0214. No third-party behavioural assumptions are used: the ALM engine applies the Bank's CPR vectors without vendor prepayment logic, and its configuration (cash-flow timing, application of prepayments to the amortisation schedule and treatment of the penalty-free allowance) is customised to the Bank's products, documented in IS-PPM-3.0 and tested in EVD-11-ITR. Non-performing loan parts are projected with the expected cash flows of the LGD workout model (MDL-02), and the scenario rate paths are generated by the ALM engine from the curves supplied by ALM/Treasury Risk. Changes in the ALM engine configuration that affect prepayment cash flows are subject to the same change management as the model.

sections.heading: Use in EVE measurement and the supervisory outlier test
sections.text: The EVE supervisory outlier test is computed quarterly for the six scenarios parallel up, parallel down, steepener, flattener, short rates up and short rates down, using the scenario-dependent CPR of PPM-NL. The Bank applies the EUR shock sizes of Part A of the Annex to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/856 (parallel 200 bp, short 250 bp, long 100 bp); no Part B calibration is needed because no other currency is material. EUR represents 98.7% of non-trading book financial assets and 97.9% of liabilities, USD (0.8%) and GBP (0.4%) are below the 5% threshold and EUR alone exceeds 90% coverage, so shocks are applied to EUR only; the model concerns EUR mortgages only. The change in EVE is computed on a run-off balance sheet in which existing loan parts amortise and prepay according to the scenario-dependent prepayment rates without new production. Cash flows are discounted with the EUR €STR OIS curve, a general risk-free curve without instrument-, sector- or entity-specific credit or liquidity spreads. As EUR is the only currency in scope, no cross-currency aggregation is needed; the ALM engine nevertheless applies the aggregation rule of Article 3(8), so a positive EVE change in a scenario is weighted by 50%.

Cash flows are discounted with the EUR €STR OIS curve, a general risk-free curve without instrument-, sector- or entity-specific credit or liquidity spreads.

As EUR is the only currency in scope, no cross-currency aggregation is needed; the ALM engine nevertheless applies the aggregation rule of Article 3(8), so a positive EVE change in a scenario is weighted by 50%.

sections.heading: Commercial margins and non-performing exposures
sections.text: For the EVE measures the Bank excludes commercial margins from the mortgage cash flows: interest cash flows are projected at the risk-free rate at inception, defined as the EUR OIS swap rate for the initial fixed-rate period at the offer date as used in FTP, applied consistently to all banking book instruments and business units and aligned with the hedging of the mortgage portfolio with OIS payer swaps; the exclusion was notified to the ECB Joint Supervisory Team on 28 June 2024. Non-performing mortgage loan parts (1.1% of the mortgage balance) are not modelled by PPM-NL but are included in EVE and NII as interest rate sensitive instruments, net of provisions, with the expected cash flows and timing of the workout model. The Bank's NPE ratio of 1.3% at 31 December 2026 is below 2%, so Article 3(4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/856 does not require the inclusion of NPEs in the SOT; they are nevertheless included to keep the SOT consistent with the internal measures. The IRRBB perimeter therefore covers all interest rate sensitive mortgage positions: performing and non-performing loan parts, the mortgage pipeline as off-balance-sheet loan commitments, and the related hedging derivatives.

sections.heading: Use in NII measurement
sections.text: The NII supervisory outlier test applies the parallel up and parallel down scenarios and covers interest income and expenses over a one-year horizon regardless of the maturity and accounting treatment of the instruments. The change in NII is computed on a constant balance sheet: prepaid, maturing and repricing mortgage balances are replaced by mortgages of the same currency, amount and fixed-rate period, priced at the average margin of new production over the last three months rather than at historical margins. The NII measures include commercial margins, and prepayment compensation received under each scenario is included in projected interest income. The NII outlier test flags a large decline where one-year NII falls by more than 5% of Tier 1 capital under either parallel scenario; with PPM-NL v3.0 the worst outcome at 31 December 2026 is −3.0% of Tier 1 capital (parallel down). The Bank uses the NII sensitivity including market value changes of fair-valued hedging instruments (NII+MV) and the EVE sensitivity, which together capture gap, basis and option risk; PPM-NL provides the option risk component of both measures.

sections.heading: Scenario-conditional application and rate floor
sections.text: Prepayment speeds respond to the rate path of each EVE, NII and SOT scenario: the refinancing incentive, the curtailment incentive and the lock-in effect on sales are recomputed monthly from the shocked offered-rate curve, so that prepayments rise in falling-rate scenarios and fall in rising-rate scenarios. After each shock, the post-shock rate floor of −150 bp at immediate maturity, rising by 3 bp per year to 0% at 50 years, is applied to the EUR risk-free curve before the offered rates and incentives are derived; where observed rates are below the floor, the observed rate is used. The application of PPM-NL to the prescribed shock scenarios, including the rate floor and the post-shock prepayment behaviour, was tested for all eight SOT scenarios in the parallel run (EVD-11-ITR section 7) and in the SOT comparison of EVD-11-BTR. IRRBB exposure is measured monthly under the internal set of 12 scenarios for changes in level and shape of the yield curve and in the basis between swap and mortgage offered rates, and the SOT quarterly. The same model and parameters are used for EVE, NII, the SOT, the ICAAP and hedging; FTP will continue to use the v2.3 CPR tables until the FTP system release planned for the first quarter of 2028.

sections.heading: Fixed-rate loans, prepayment compensation and pipeline
sections.text: For fixed-rate mortgage loan parts, the scenario-dependent prepayment rates, the rate-reset behaviour and the prepayment compensation are applied in every IRRBB measure; for fixed-rate loan commitments the expected take-up of the pipeline component is applied in all measures. The projection reflects the contractual prepayment conditions: a penalty-free allowance of 10% of the original principal per calendar year applies to all loan parts, prepayments at sale, death and at the end of the fixed-rate period are penalty-free, and other prepayments above the allowance pay compensation equal to the present value of the difference between the contract rate and the Bank's offered rate for the remaining fixed-rate period; the compensation received is included in projected NII and in the EVE cash flows. The pipeline take-up component estimates the probability that an offer is drawn as a logistic function of the change in the offered rate for the same fixed-rate period since the offer date and the remaining offer validity (offers are valid for six months, with the day-rate option that the borrower receives the lower of the offered and the prevailing rate at drawdown). Pipeline exposures are included in EVE, NII and the hedging strategy from the offer date with the expected take-up under each rate scenario, and the Treasury ALM desk hedges the expected pipeline with forward-starting payer swaps.

sections.heading: Development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: Before estimation, the samples were defined as follows: the development window is January 2012 to December 2024; within it, 25% of mortgage loans were drawn at random (seed 20261109) as out-of-sample hold-out, and the out-of-time sample is January to December 2025 (12.1 million loan-part-months). The out-of-time sample was not used for variable selection or parameter estimation; the final coefficients are those estimated on the 75% development sample. The development sample contains 118.9 million loan-part-months, 160,810 full prepayments and 965,200 partial prepayments; the out-of-sample hold-out contains 39.6 million loan-part-months. The development window contains the rising-rate period of 2022–2023, so that the out-of-the-money response is estimated on observed behaviour.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Four methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements of ALM-STD-400 §6, data requirements, out-of-time accuracy, stability of the incentive response, interpretability and implementability in the ALM engine): (1) CPR look-up tables by incentive and seasoning bucket as in v2.3; (2) a Cox proportional hazards model; (3) a multinomial logit model; and (4) gradient-boosted trees. The look-up tables could not separate sale from refinancing and showed a 2025 out-of-time CPR error of +1.8 percentage points; the Cox model had a similar fit to the logit (AUC 0.719 against 0.726) but requires a baseline hazard that cannot be projected per scenario without additional assumptions; gradient-boosted trees improved the out-of-time AUC by only 0.006 and would be less transparent. The multinomial logit model was selected because it models the competing outcomes jointly, gives interpretable driver effects that can be challenged by Treasury, performs at least as well as the alternatives out of time, and can be applied per scenario in the projection module; the more complex gradient-boosted alternative was rejected as its small performance gain does not justify the loss of transparency.

sections.heading: Model specification
sections.text: For loan part i in month t, the probability of outcome k ∈ {partial prepayment, full prepayment at sale, full prepayment for refinancing} is P(k) = exp(β_k·x_it) / (1 + Σ_j exp(β_j·x_it)), with no prepayment as the reference outcome. The driver vector x_it contains segment intercepts, linear splines of the refinancing incentive, seasoning splines, the remaining penalty-free allowance, a December indicator, the curtailment incentive, borrower age band, the 12-month change in the regional house price index, indexed LTV bucket, remaining fixed-rate period bucket, a burnout variable, NHG indicator and loan size bucket. Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood with robust standard errors clustered by mortgage loan, using statsmodels MNLogit. The monthly probabilities are aggregated into the SMM per segment and scenario and converted to annual CPR.

sections.heading: Candidate drivers and variable selection
sections.text: Thirty-one candidate drivers were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the monthly production run and stability of their effect over 2012–2018 against 2019–2024; eight were rejected, for example the borrower's employment status (not available at the point of use) and the 3-month change in Euribor (effect not stable over time). Variable selection combined univariate analysis (information value per outcome), stepwise multivariate selection by likelihood-ratio test at 1% significance, and a correlation analysis in which, of pairs with a correlation above 0.6 (for example loan age and seasoning since the last rate reset), only the driver with the stronger economic rationale was retained. The final model uses as drivers the refinancing incentive, loan seasoning, the remaining penalty-free allowance, and relocation and property sale through borrower age, the regional house price change and the rate lock-in effect. Selection decisions that required judgement, such as the knot positions of the incentive spline, are recorded in the expert judgement log (chapter 11).

sections.heading: Final coefficients and economic rationale
sections.text: Every final driver has a sign and magnitude consistent with economic intuition: for refinancing, the incentive coefficient is +1.08 per 100 bp above the +50 bp knot and +0.21 per 100 bp between −100 bp and +50 bp, reflecting the threshold created by prepayment compensation; burnout reduces refinancing by −0.34 per year of cumulative in-the-money exposure; for sale, the house price change coefficient is +0.021 per percentage point, the lock-in effect is −0.18 per 100 bp of negative incentive and borrowers aged 25–34 move more often (+0.41 against age 45–54); for partial prepayment, the December indicator is +1.37, the remaining allowance +0.88 and the curtailment incentive +0.29 per 100 bp. All retained coefficients are significant at the 1% level; the full coefficient table with standard errors is given in Annex 1 and in the parameter file ppm_v3_coefficients.csv (parameter set PPM-PARAM-3.0.2). The resulting model reflects the effect of the interest rate scenario (incentive, lock-in and curtailment incentive), the economic environment (house prices and savings rates) and contractual features (penalty-free allowance, compensation, fixed-rate period and NHG) on current and future prepayment speeds.

sections.heading: Partial prepayment amount and rate reset
sections.text: Component B models the prepaid amount, as a share of the outstanding balance, given a partial prepayment, with a fractional logit on the remaining allowance, December indicator, age band and loan size; the median prepaid share is 4.8% and 71% of partial prepayments fall within the penalty-free allowance. Component C models, at the end of the fixed-rate period, the probability that the loan part is redeemed (on average 6.8% of resets in 2016–2025) as a logistic function of the difference between the Bank's offered rate and the market average rate, and the choice of the new fixed-rate period (2016–2025 average: 10 years 46%, 20 years 22%, 5 years 18%, one year or variable 14%) as a multinomial logit on the slope of the offered-rate curve. Internal refinancing through rate averaging during the fixed-rate period is treated as a refinancing event, because the loan part reprices to a new fixed-rate period. Both components are re-evaluated per scenario in the projection.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The calibration target is the realised monthly prepayment rate per segment on the development sample; the maximum likelihood estimates reproduce the in-sample full and partial prepayment rates per segment within 0.5% relative, so no separate recalibration step is applied. Prepayment parameters are calibrated on 13 years of loan-level history (2012–2024) and are recalibrated when the annual back-testing shows a structural deviation, defined as a red back-testing result in two consecutive years or in the latest year for the portfolio. At 31 December 2025, the model gives a base-case CPR of 5.3% for the portfolio: 5.6% for S1, 4.4% for S2 and 4.9% for S3. By incentive bucket, the base-case CPR ranges from 3.1% for loan parts more than 100 bp out of the money to 12.1% for loan parts more than 100 bp in the money; by seasoning, from 2.4% in the first year to 6.2% after five years.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: Performance was tested on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples for discriminatory power (AUC per outcome), calibration accuracy (predicted against realised CPR) and stability (PSI and coefficient stability), with metrics and thresholds consistent with MV-HB-003 and the monitoring plan. sections.heading: Stress testing of behavioural assumptions
sections.text: For the Bank's stress-testing framework (ERM-STD-300), PPM-NL provides behavioural stress variants in which customer behaviour changes: a CPR halving under a housing market freeze and a CPR doubling under an aggressive refinancing wave, which are included in the ICAAP adverse scenario. The largest EVE effect is the CPR halving in the parallel up scenario (−EUR 143 million).

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material model assumptions have been identified and assessed for plausibility: (a) borrower behaviour observed in 2012–2024 is representative of future behaviour conditional on the drivers; (b) the incentive response is stable and can be applied to shocked rate paths up to the observed incentive range; (c) the Bank's offered rate follows the swap curve with a constant margin in all scenarios; (d) the penalty-free allowance and compensation rules remain unchanged; (e) the intended use is portfolio-level projection and not loan-level prediction. The key behavioural assumptions are documented in this MDD, justified by the Bank's historical data (chapters 4, 5 and 7), aligned with the mortgage business strategy agreed with Mortgage Product Management, and tested annually through back-testing and sensitivity analysis; the materiality thresholds of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/857 are applied proportionately to decide which assumptions are modelled per scenario. All model inputs, assumptions and specification choices are documented and explained in chapters 3, 4 and 8 so that they are included in the independent validation.

sections.heading: Implementation

Red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the Model Risk Committee.

sections.heading: Scope and approach
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the reference data set RDS-PPM-NL-2026.1 for the Mortgage Prepayment Model NL (PPM-NL v3.0, model MDL-11), performed by ALM Modelling with the Data Stewards of the Retail Mortgages, Credit Risk Data, Collateral and Market Data domains between 5 and 30 October 2026. The assessment applies the Data Quality Standard for Models (MRM-STD-022) to all 17 critical data elements and to the RDS as a whole, before model estimation, and its results feed chapter 6 of the RDS documentation EVD-11-RDS. Data quality is assessed on completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, complemented by validity and uniqueness. Report version 1.0 was approved by the model owner on 4 November 2026.

sections.heading: Critical data elements and rule inventory
sections.text: The 17 CDEs are: loan-part identifier, product code, repayment type, origination date, original principal, contractual principal outstanding, scheduled amortisation, contract rate, fixed-rate end date, redemption amount, redemption transaction code, redemption reason code, NHG indicator, indexed market value, borrower date of birth, offered rate per fixed-rate period, and the regional house price index. For each CDE at least one DQ rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension, 96 rules in total (completeness 31, accuracy 22, consistency 25, timeliness 12, validity 4, uniqueness 2), and the reason is recorded where a dimension is not applicable, for example timeliness for the static origination attributes. The rules were defined jointly with the Data Stewards, are documented in Annex A of the RDS documentation and, for the 71 recurring rules, implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool (rule set DQM-ALM-PPM).

The only deviation is the relaxed completeness threshold for the redemption reason code in 2012–2015 (amber below 80%, red below 70%), justified by the historical gap DD-01 and approved by the model owner on 21 October 2026 and, because PPM-NL is Tier 1, by Model Risk Management on 23 October 2026 (MRM-DEV-2026-044). No other threshold is less strict than the default.

sections.text: As required for Tier 1 models, 250 prepayment events drawn at random from 2016–2025 (150 full and 100 partial prepayments, stratified by segment) were verified against source documentation: redemption statements, notary settlement statements for sales and customer instructions for partial prepayments. The redemption amount and date were confirmed for all 250 events; the redemption reason code was confirmed for 247 events (98.8%), and three events coded as refinancing were in fact sales, which Mortgage Operations corrected in MAS on 27 October 2026. The error rate is within the accuracy expectation agreed with the Data Owner, and the finding is recorded under DD-01.

sections.heading: Scope and implementation specification
sections.text: This report documents the implementation and testing of PPM-NL v3.0 (model MDL-11) in the production service ppm-engine and the Bank's ALM engine, performed between 1 February and 28 May 2027. The implementation follows specification IS-PPM-3.0 v1.0, which is consistent with the MDD and was approved by the model owner on 29 March 2027, before implementation of the production code started. IS-PPM-3.0 defines every transformation, missing value and outlier treatment, formula, coefficient, spline knot, floor and cap with precision and rounding conventions, and states that the penalty-free allowance of 10% of the original principal per calendar year is applied to all loan parts in the cash-flow projection. The report was approved by the model owner on 4 June 2027.

sections.text: Implementation testing was performed by the Model Implementation Testing team of Risk IT, which is independent of the author of the production code and, as PPM-NL is Tier 1, of the model development team. The test plan TP-PPM-3.0 defined unit tests of the transformations, integration tests of the interface to the ALM engine, output reconciliation, a parallel run and user acceptance testing. sections.heading: Test cases and results
sections.text: All 186 test cases of IS-PPM-3.0 were executed, covering the input mapping and transformations, the handling of missing, invalid and boundary values (incentive at the spline knots, allowance fully used, indexed LTV at the 250% cap, missing age band), and the outputs for every segment and all eight SOT scenarios. The test plan, cases, results and defects are documented in this report: 183 cases passed at the first run, and three defects affecting outputs (wrong day-count in the compensation calculation, December indicator in leap years and the rate floor for maturities beyond 30 years) were resolved and retested successfully before the parallel run. No open defects remain that affect model outputs.

documents.title: Prepayment back-testing, benchmarking and sensitivity report 2026

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This report presents the 2026 annual back-testing of the production prepayment model PPM-NL v2.3, the out-of-time back-testing and benchmarking of the redeveloped model v3.0, the sensitivity of EVE and NII to the key behavioural assumptions, the SOT comparison of both versions and the ICAAP model risk add-on. It is prepared by ALM Modelling under ALM-STD-400 §8 and was presented to ALCO on 11 May 2027. Reference data are the RDS-PPM-NL-2026.1 data up to December 2025 and the monthly production data up to March 2027.

sections.heading: Back-testing framework and thresholds
sections.text: Back-testing compares predicted and realised prepayment rates per cohort (origination year and fixed-rate period), segment and product, predicted and realised pipeline take-up, and modelled and realised prepayment compensation, at least annually. The thresholds are derived from the traffic-light approach of MV-HB-003 and documented in the MDD: relative deviation of the annual CPR per segment up to 15% green, 15–30% amber, above 30% red; absolute portfolio deviation above 1.0 percentage point amber and above 2.0 red; a red outcome triggers recalibration or a rationale approved by ALCO. Deviations are computed on the base-case projection made at the start of each year with the realised rate path.

documents.title: Model change memorandum – PPM-NL v2.3 to v3.0 (CHG-2026-031)

sections.heading: Change description and rationale
sections.text: This memorandum describes the redevelopment of the Mortgage Prepayment Model NL from v2.3 to v3.0: replacement of the CPR look-up tables by a multinomial logit model separating partial prepayment, full prepayment at sale and full prepayment for refinancing, a new rate-reset component, integration of the pipeline take-up model and removal of overlay PMA-ALM-2023-02; the rationale is the red back-testing of v2.3 in 2024 and 2025, the High validation finding of April 2026 and MRC condition C-2026-017; the affected components are the methodology, the RDS, the parameters and the projection module, and the affected documents are the RDS documentation, the MDD, IS-PPM-3.0 and the user guide. The memorandum also records the classification, quantitative impact, required validation and implementation plan.

sections.text: The change is classified by internal materiality; PPM-NL does not require supervisory permission, so no regulatory class applies.
